key_insight: On a 3D expansion-compression cone, the shock/boundary-layer interaction shifts from corner-locked, large separation at low Reynolds number to a smaller, downstream-moving bubble with faster but weaker shear-layer flapping as the incoming boundary layer becomes more developed.
engineering_relevance: Understanding how shock location and separation dynamics change with transition state is critical for designing hypersonic vehicles and control surfaces that must tolerate heating, loads, and unsteady pressure in non-canonical geometries.
method: High-frequency pressure sensors and high-framerate schlieren to capture unsteady shock motion.
Temperature-sensitive paint, shear-stress measurements, and oil-flow visualization to map separation and surface transport.
Tests at Mach 5 and 8 with Reynolds number variation to span laminar, transitional, and turbulent approach boundary layers.
evidence_signal: The abstract reports consistent experimental trends across Mach 5 and 8: shock attachment location, separation size, shear-layer flapping frequency/amplitude, and low-frequency breathing motions all vary systematically with Reynolds number and boundary-layer state.
watch_item: Because strong relaminarization at Mach 8 prevents fully turbulent interaction behavior, results may not transfer directly to canonical turbulent shock/boundary-layer models.
paper_title: Hypersonic Shock-Wave/Boundary-Layer Interaction on a Three-Dimensional Expansion-Compression Geometry
